content.heading: 6.0  Where the LLM becomes a doer
content.body:
This is the chapter where the LLM stops being a talker and becomes a doer. Tool use — also called function calling — is the single most important mechanism in agentic AI. It is the bridge that lets a model's DECISIONS trigger your real code: looking something up, running a calculation, calling an API, reading a file.

Everything in Chapters 1-5 was preparation for this. Understand it deeply and the idea of an "agent" becomes concrete rather than magical.
content.callout: Function calling is the single most important mechanism in agentic AI.

content.heading: 6.1  The one thing everyone misunderstands at first
content.body:
Read this slowly, because it is the crux: the model does NOT run your code. It only REQUESTS that your code be run.

Here is the flow, in plain words. First, you tell the model, up front, which tools exist — their names, what each one does, and what information each one needs. Second, if the model decides a tool would help, it produces a structured REQUEST that says, in effect, "please run the function get_weather with the city set to Tokyo." It does not execute anything. It just emits that request as data. Third, YOUR system reads that request, actually runs the real function, and gets a result. Fourth, you hand the result back to the model. Fifth, the model uses the result to decide its next step or to write its final answer.

Notice this is exactly the structured-output skill from Chapter 5, now given a formal channel. The model producing "call get_weather with city=Tokyo" is just the model producing well-shaped data. Function calling IS structured output, specialized for the purpose of requesting actions.

A comparison that will click for you: think of the model as producing a Command object — a little package naming an action and its arguments. The model is the planner that fills out the command; your own dispatcher receives it and carries it out, then reports back. The model never touches the machinery; it only decides what should happen.
content.callout: The model REQUESTS an action; your code EXECUTES it. It is the Command pattern, applied to agents.

content.heading: 6.2  How a tool is described to the model
content.body: For the model to use a tool wisely, it must be told about it. A tool description includes three things: the tool's NAME, a plain-language description of WHAT IT DOES (and when to use it), and a specification of the INFORMATION IT NEEDS (its parameters, with their types).
content.snippet:
name: get_weather
does: "Get the current weather for a city. Use this whenever the user
       asks about weather or what to wear or pack."
needs:
    city  (text)   - the city name, for example "Tokyo"
    unit  (text)   - either "celsius" or "fahrenheit"
content.snippetExplanation: What this shows: The model learns there is a tool called get_weather, learns from the plain-language "does" line WHEN it is appropriate to reach for it, and learns it must supply a city and optionally a unit. The "either/or" on the unit is like a fixed set of allowed values — it narrows the model's choices and prevents nonsense. And here is the most important craft point in the chapter: the DESCRIPTION is not decoration — it is the real interface between you and the model. The model decides whether and how to use a tool almost entirely based on that description. Vague descriptions are the number-one cause of bad tool use. Write them the way you would document a public method for a new teammate: say clearly what it does, say when to use it (and when not), and describe each input with examples and allowed values.
content.callout: A tool's description IS its interface. Vague descriptions are the number-one cause of bad tool use.

content.heading: 6.3  The full cycle, in plain English
content.body:
Let us trace one complete interaction where the user asks, "What's the weather in Tokyo, and should I bring an umbrella?" and the model has the get_weather tool.

First, USER asks the question. You send it, along with the list of available tools, to the model. Second, the model responds — but not with an answer. It responds with a REQUEST: "run get_weather with city = Tokyo." (Recall from Chapter 3 that the "finish reason" on this response would be "tool_calls.") Third, YOUR system sees that request and actually calls the real weather function, which returns something like: rain, 80% chance, 18 degrees. Fourth, you add that result to the conversation as a message with the TOOL role, and send the conversation back to the model. Fifth, now the model has the real data and writes its final answer.

There is a pattern here worth naming, because every tool interaction is built from it.
content.snippet:
user      -> the question
assistant -> a tool request (not an answer)
tool      -> the result your code produced
assistant -> the final answer, informed by the result
content.snippetExplanation: What this shows: This four-step pattern — request, then result, then answer — is the atom of tool use. More complex agents simply repeat it (Chapter 7).
content.callout: Request, then result, then answer — the four-step atom of every tool interaction.

content.heading: 6.4  Details that trip people up
content.body:
You will not be wiring these by hand yet, but understanding them makes you fluent.

THE MODEL'S REQUEST MUST STAY IN THE CONVERSATION. When you send the tool's result back, the model needs to see its own earlier request alongside it, so it can connect the answer to the question it asked. Dropping that link confuses the model.

RESULTS GO BACK AS TEXT. Tool results are handed back as text (typically JSON text). The model reads them as more context to reason over.

THE MODEL CAN ASK FOR SEVERAL TOOLS AT ONCE. In a single turn it might request two or three tool calls together (say, weather AND local time). Your system runs them all and returns all the results.

THE ARGUMENTS THE MODEL SUPPLIES ARE UNTRUSTED. The model can get an argument wrong or even invent a nonsensical one. You must treat tool arguments exactly like untrusted input to a REST endpoint — validate them before acting. This is a direct application of Chapter 5's Level-3 validation idea, and it matters enormously for safety.
content.callout: Tool arguments produced by the model are UNTRUSTED input. Validate them before acting — always.

content.heading: 6.5  What makes a good tool
content.body:
Designing tools well is a real skill. The principles: ONE CLEAR PURPOSE per tool — a tool should do one well-defined thing. A GREAT DESCRIPTION (6.2) — the model's behavior hinges on it. CONSTRAINED INPUTS — use fixed sets of allowed values and mark which inputs are required, to shrink the room for mistakes. CONCISE, STRUCTURED RESULTS — return what the model needs, not a giant blob; a tool that dumps 100,000 tokens of output floods the finite context "desk" (Chapter 2), so summarize or paginate large results. INFORMATIVE FAILURES — when something goes wrong, return a clear message the model can act on ("city not found — ask the user to clarify") rather than simply crashing. FEW, DISTINCT TOOLS — too many overlapping tools confuse the model about which to pick; a small, well-chosen set beats a sprawling one.

A guiding thought: an agent is only as good as the tools you give it and the descriptions you write for them. The model is the decision-maker; the tools are its hands. Dull or confusing hands make for a clumsy agent no matter how clever the model.
content.callout: The model is the decision-maker; tools are its hands. Few, distinct, well-described tools beat a sprawling set.

content.heading: 6.6  Tools are power, and power needs safety
content.body:
The instant a model can trigger real actions, safety stops being optional. This is a theme we develop fully in Chapter 16, but it begins here, because it begins with tools.

VALIDATE EVERYTHING THE MODEL SENDS. Never pass model-produced arguments straight into anything consequential. Check them first — the same discipline you apply to user input in a web controller.

LEAST PRIVILEGE. A tool should be able to do the narrowest thing possible. Do not expose a "run any database command" tool; expose "look up an order by its id." Do not expose "run any shell command"; expose specific, bounded operations. The less a tool CAN do, the less can go wrong.

NEVER FEED MODEL TEXT DIRECTLY INTO DANGEROUS OPERATIONS. Things like database queries, shell commands, file paths, or arbitrary web requests must be constructed carefully and safely — exactly as you would guard against injection attacks in a normal application.

REQUIRE HUMAN APPROVAL FOR HIGH-STAKES ACTIONS. For anything irreversible or expensive — deleting data, sending money, emailing customers — insert a human checkpoint (Chapter 16). The agent proposes; a person approves.

The rule of thumb: design every tool as if a confused or even malicious party is supplying its arguments — because, through a fooled model, one effectively might be. Security in agentic systems lives in your CODE and your PERMISSIONS, not in polite requests to the model.
content.callout: Security lives in your code and permissions, not in polite requests to the model.

content.heading: 6.7  One round isn't enough — which points to the loop
content.body:
The cycle in 6.3 handles a single round: the model asks for tools, you run them, the model answers. But many real tasks need MORE than one round. Consider: "Find the cheapest flight to Tokyo next Friday, then check the weather there that day, and tell me what to pack."

To handle this, the model must: search flights, SEE the chosen date, THEN look up the weather for that specific date, THEN reason, THEN answer. That is tool, then observe, then another tool, then observe, then answer. A single request-and-result cannot express an unknown number of rounds. What you need is a LOOP that keeps going as long as the model keeps asking for tools, and stops when it finally produces an answer.

That loop — think, act, observe, repeat — is precisely the agent loop from Chapter 1. You are now exactly one loop away from a real agent, and that loop is the entire subject of the next chapter.
content.callout: A single tool round cannot express an unknown number of steps. You are one loop away from a real agent.

content.heading: Check your understanding
content.body:
For reflection, not coding.

1. A colleague says, "The AI ran a database query for me." Correct them: what actually happened, step by step?

2. Why is a tool's plain-language DESCRIPTION described as "the real interface"? What tends to happen when it is vague?

3. Recite the four-step atom of tool use (user, assistant, tool, assistant) and explain what each step contains.

4. Why must tool arguments produced by the model be treated as untrusted, and how does this connect to Chapter 5's idea of validation?

5. Explain "least privilege" for tools with your own example of a safe versus unsafe tool design.

6. Why does a single request-and-result cycle fail for a task like "find a flight, then check that day's weather, then advise" — and what does that imply we need next?
content.callout: Next chapter: the agent loop itself — ReAct and reasoning, the conceptual heart of the book.
